messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: "Warning: slice sampler reached..."
parts:
Hi Jose,

It's hard to say.  This is a trap we added in the last release to try to catch conditions when the slice sampler is in a bad state, which could conceivably lead to an infinite loop.  This could occur if there is a bad initial condition, or something is invalid (NaN or Inf) in the model, or there is a bimodal conditional distribution.  Is it happening early in the MCMC or late, once or many times?  Is it a univariate slice sampler or part of the AF_slice sampler?  If it is univariate, you could try replacing it with a RW (random walk Metropolis-Hastings).  Most of the core team is in one state of travel or another, but you could send us more about the example (on-list or off-list) if you're still stuck and we'll look at it but perhaps not right away.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: "Warning: slice sampler reached..."
parts:
Many thanks to Jose for sharing a reproducible example off-list.  For the benefit of other list readers, here is a simplified summary of what happened.

There was a case like:

for(i in 1:N) {
   a[i] ~ dpois(lambda)
   b[i] ~ dbin(p, a[i])
}

where a[i] are random effects and b[i] are data.

The initial values for a[i] did not ensure that every a[i] >= b[i].  As a result, some of the binomial log probabilities could start at -Inf, and the slice sampler for a corresponding a[i] couldn't get started.

We'll have to give some thought to handling such a case (any suggestions?).  In the meantime, please be aware that sometimes alarming behavior from nimble is simply the result of incomplete or problematic initial values.

Thanks again to Jose for the helpful example.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: "Warning: slice sampler reached..."
parts:
Guillaume, thanks for your email, and your continued interest and usage of NIMBLE.

To answer your question, no, there has not been progress on this issue of initial values with the slice sampling algorithm.  In brief, NIMBLE's MCMC (just the same as other MCMC engines) requires a "valid" starting point for the MCMC chain, manifested as a "valid" (that is, self-consistent) set of initial values for the model.  The MCMC (nor the individual sampling algorithms which comprise the MCMC, i.e., the slice sampler) is not designed nor intended to "find" a valid starting point for you.  (rather, the MCMC's goal is to *transition between* valid model states, eventually converging to the joint posterior distribution).  Point being, no, there has been no work towards an automated solution for this problem, of finding a valid initial state (a self-consistent set of model values); that it still a prerequisite of using the MCMC.

All that said, if we can be of assistance and you're able to share your code and current best attempt at finding a valid starting state, then I suspect someone on this list might be able to help point out where the problem is coming from (e.g., which model value(s) are generating the inconsistencies), and help get you on the right track.

I hope that helps.  Keep in touch.

Daniel

Dear Guillaume,

 

As Daniel said, it looks like a inits definition issue. In the original case I asked about, it was solved using inits that was consistent with data (and self-consistent, of course).

I simulated your question (see below) and changing the inits values in open HDS 9.5 code. It seems to work.

 

Best regards,

Jose

 

 

# Bundle and summarize the data set

nobs <- apply(y4d, c(1,3,4), sum)  # Total detections per site and occasion

str( data <- list(y4d=y4d, midpt=midpt, habitat=habitat, nobs = nobs) )

 

str(constants<-list(B=B, nsites=nsites, K=K, nD=nD, delta=delta, T=tmp$nyears))

 

y4d[sample(1:length(y4d), 100, replace = FALSE)] <- NA

 

# Inits

Navail.st <- apply(y4d, c(1,3,4),sum, na.rm=TRUE)

Mst <- apply(Navail.st, c( 1,3), max) + 100 # instead of + 2

inits <- list(M=Mst, Navail = Navail.st, sigma = 1.0, phi=.9,beta0=log(2),beta1=.5)

 

params <- c("sigma", "phi", "beta0", "mean.lam", "beta.trend",

   "beta1", "Mtot", "Ntot")

 

# Compile and run using NIMBLE

start.time<-Sys.time()

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code=code,

                      constants=constants,

                      data=data,

                      inits=inits,

                      check=FALSE)

 

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel,monitors=params, thin=10, useConjugacy = TRUE)

 

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

 

outNim <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, niter = 10000 , nburnin = 5000 , nchains = 1, inits=inits,

                  setSeed = TRUE, progressBar = TRUE, samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)

 

summary(outNim)

# the guilties were here:

                    K = nrep.fa,

Guillaume, thanks for your email, and your continued interest and usage of NIMBLE.

 

To answer your question, no, there has not been progress on this issue of initial values with the slice sampling algorithm.  In brief, NIMBLE's MCMC (just the same as other MCMC engines) requires a "valid" starting point for the MCMC chain, manifested as a "valid" (that is, self-consistent) set of initial values for the model.  The MCMC (nor the individual sampling algorithms which comprise the MCMC, i.e., the slice sampler) is not designed nor intended to "find" a valid starting point for you.  (rather, the MCMC's goal is to *transition between* valid model states, eventually converging to the joint posterior distribution).  Point being, no, there has been no work towards an automated solution for this problem, of finding a valid initial state (a self-consistent set of model values); that it still a prerequisite of using the MCMC.

 

All that said, if we can be of assistance and you're able to share your code and current best attempt at finding a valid starting state, then I suspect someone on this list might be able to help point out where the problem is coming from (e.g., which model value(s) are generating the inconsistencies), and help get you on the right track.

Daniel

Dear Quresh,

Thanks for posting the question.

It's hard to say without seeing more about your initial values.  In general, nimble is sensitive to the need for valid initial values, and there are cases where JAGS can recover but nimble can't recover.  Here is an example of how your initial values could potentially cause a problem.  If Z[j,i] is 0, then z[j, i] == n.point[j] is impossible and will have log probability of -Inf.  Sometimes an MCMC can recover from invalid initial values, sometimes not.  If psi[j, i] comes from an inverse logit, there can be numerical underflow that makes psi[j,i] exactly zero instead of just very very small, and that could also cause such a problem.  

You can use the nimble model in R to investigate where you have a problem (but you will have to use nimbleModel explicitly, not simply nimbleMCMC).  If model is the object returned from nimbleModel, you can explore it like:
model$calculate() # check if the entire model is valid
model$calculate("z")
model$calculate( model$expandNodeNames("z[1, ]") )
model$calculate("z[1, 1]") # These are examples of calculating the sum of log probabilities for parts of a model to see where there might be a problem.
model$z # inspect model variables, especially values such as psi[j, i] and Z[j, i] to see if anything is being set to 0

The user manual has more about how you can use models.

I hope that helps.  If you investigate further and you're still stuck, please provide a reproducible example either on-list or off-list.

Perry

Guillaume, thanks for your email, and your continued interest and usage of NIMBLE.

 

To answer your question, no, there has not been progress on this issue of initial values with the slice sampling algorithm.  In brief, NIMBLE's MCMC (just the same as other MCMC engines) requires a "valid" starting point for the MCMC chain, manifested as a "valid" (that is, self-consistent) set of initial values for the model.  The MCMC (nor the individual sampling algorithms which comprise the MCMC, i.e., the slice sampler) is not designed nor intended to "find" a valid starting point for you.  (rather, the MCMC's goal is to *transition between* valid model states, eventually converging to the joint posterior distribution).  Point being, no, there has been no work towards an automated solution for this problem, of finding a valid initial state (a self-consistent set of model values); that it still a prerequisite of using the MCMC.

 

All that said, if we can be of assistance and you're able to share your code and current best attempt at finding a valid starting state, then I suspect someone on this list might be able to help point out where the problem is coming from (e.g., which model value(s) are generating the inconsistencies), and help get you on the right track.

Dear Quresh,

Thanks for posting the question.

It's hard to say without seeing more about your initial values.  In general, nimble is sensitive to the need for valid initial values, and there are cases where JAGS can recover but nimble can't recover.  Here is an example of how your initial values could potentially cause a problem.  If Z[j,i] is 0, then z[j, i] == n.point[j] is impossible and will have log probability of -Inf.  Sometimes an MCMC can recover from invalid initial values, sometimes not.  If psi[j, i] comes from an inverse logit, there can be numerical underflow that makes psi[j,i] exactly zero instead of just very very small, and that could also cause such a problem.  

You can use the nimble model in R to investigate where you have a problem (but you will have to use nimbleModel explicitly, not simply nimbleMCMC).  If model is the object returned from nimbleModel, you can explore it like:
model$calculate() # check if the entire model is valid
model$calculate("z")
model$calculate( model$expandNodeNames("z[1, ]") )
model$calculate("z[1, 1]") # These are examples of calculating the sum of log probabilities for parts of a model to see where there might be a problem.
model$z # inspect model variables, especially values such as psi[j, i] and Z[j, i] to see if anything is being set to 0

The user manual has more about how you can use models.

I hope that helps.  If you investigate further and you're still stuck, please provide a reproducible example either on-list or off-list.

Perry

Guillaume, thanks for your email, and your continued interest and usage of NIMBLE.

 

To answer your question, no, there has not been progress on this issue of initial values with the slice sampling algorithm.  In brief, NIMBLE's MCMC (just the same as other MCMC engines) requires a "valid" starting point for the MCMC chain, manifested as a "valid" (that is, self-consistent) set of initial values for the model.  The MCMC (nor the individual sampling algorithms which comprise the MCMC, i.e., the slice sampler) is not designed nor intended to "find" a valid starting point for you.  (rather, the MCMC's goal is to *transition between* valid model states, eventually converging to the joint posterior distribution).  Point being, no, there has been no work towards an automated solution for this problem, of finding a valid initial state (a self-consistent set of model values); that it still a prerequisite of using the MCMC.

 

All that said, if we can be of assistance and you're able to share your code and current best attempt at finding a valid starting state, then I suspect someone on this list might be able to help point out where the problem is coming from (e.g., which model value(s) are generating the inconsistencies), and help get you on the right track.

Many thanks to Jose for sharing a reproducible example off-list.  For the benefit of other list readers, here is a simplified summary of what happened.

 

There was a case like:

 

for(i in 1:N) {

   a[i] ~ dpois(lambda)

   b[i] ~ dbin(p, a[i])
}

 

where a[i] are random effects and b[i] are data.

 

The initial values for a[i] did not ensure that every a[i] >= b[i].  As a result, some of the binomial log probabilities could start at -Inf, and the slice sampler for a corresponding a[i] couldn't get started.

 

We'll have to give some thought to handling such a case (any suggestions?).  In the meantime, please be aware that sometimes alarming behavior from nimble is simply the result of incomplete or problematic initial values.

 

Thanks again to Jose for the helpful example.
